extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO discipline counsel, and adjudicators in PTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating alleged misconduct by practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office under 37 C.F.R. § 10.23 (dishonesty, prejudicial conduct, fitness to practice, and false statements to the Office). Used in disciplinary pleadings, motions, and hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudicial to the administration of justice (Rule 10.23(b)(5) standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prejudicial to the administration of justice" means that the act "hampered the efficient and proper operation of the courts or of ancillary systems upon which the courts rely," (citing Iowa Supreme Ct. Bd. of Prof'l Ethics & Conduct v. Steffes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/indicia: creating or using a fabricated demonstrative exhibit (GX 2195) without disclosure; failing to inform the tribunal or opposing counsel of the exhibit's origin; depriving opposing counsel of an opportunity to rehabilitate a witness; undermining the deposition process; causing confusion that prevents full elicitation of relevant facts; wasting time and judicial/administrative resources (motions, conference calls, rulings); undermining the tribunal's ability to control proceedings; potential to induce settlements based on misleading evidence. The lack of a specific rule on demonstrative aids does not authorize conduct that violates this broad prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not "engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete forms: creating false evidence, introducing fabricated documents into proceedings, making deceptive or evasive statements to opposing counsel or tribunal, filing false or misleading declarations. The Board and OED characterize use of fabricated GX 2195 and evasive/email responses as falling squarely within this prohibition. Cited authorities and prior findings (e.g., ITC/Federal Circuit determinations of misrepresentation/inequitable conduct) are relevant background evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on fitness to practice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not "engage in any other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation/Limitation: To constitute "other" conduct under §10.23(b)(6), the conduct must not already be prohibited by §§10.23(b)(1)-(5) (Moatz v. Colitz). Thus (b)(6) cannot be invoked to punish the same conduct already covered by (b)(4) or (b)(5). The Complaint may plead (b)(6) in the alternative, but proof must identify conduct distinct from the specific prohibitions of (b)(1)-(5). OED's theory that conduct violating (b)(4)/(b)(5) also violates (b)(6) is rejected where there is no separate misconduct beyond what the other paragraphs cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to the Office or its employees (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(c)(2)(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct which constitutes a violation includes "knowingly giving false or misleading information or knowingly participating in a material way in giving false or misleading information" to "The Office or any employee of the Office."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative application: a practitioner's written assertion to OED that his "fitness to practice has never been called into question" when, in fact, there are prior judicial findings (e.g., ITC/Federal Circuit) or OED communications that call it into question. Key elements in dispute: knowledge (did the practitioner know the statement was false?) and whether materiality is required (OED argues materiality is not required; respondent argues materiality is an element for false-statement offenses). Case law and Model Rules commentary are invoked by both sides to support their positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose origin of demonstrative/fabricated exhibits or obtain tribunal permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Although no specific interference-rule governs demonstrative aids, the absence of a rule does not authorize use of demonstrative aids in a way that violates broad prohibitions (e.g., conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice). OED's position: where there are no rules, statutes or case law authorizing presenting a fabricated document, the practitioner should have given the Board the opportunity to consider whether the ruse was appropriate and to issue orders to prevent misleading the Board or opposing counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectations: disclose the demonstrative's origin (or obtain Board/tribunal consent) before or at least promptly after use; failure to do so can undermine the tribunal's ability to control the proceeding and to protect fact-finding (e.g., redirect/rehabilitation). Expert testimony and Board findings emphasize that withholding such information to prevent rebuttal is prejudicial and contrary to trial norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for the fact-finding process: opportunity for redirect/rehabilitation of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Redirect examination following cross-examination is an important part of the fact-finding process; denying opposing counsel a fair opportunity to rehabilitate a witness is inconsistent with trial process norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: tactics designed to prevent rehabilitation (e.g., withholding that an exhibit is demonstrative or fabricated until after deposition/transcript) can taint witness testimony and lead to findings that the practitioner's conduct is prejudicial to administration of justice. Expert witnesses in the record stress the centrality of redirect for accurate fact-finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct inconsistent with PTO's mandate of just, speedy, and inexpensive determination (37 C.F.R. § 1.601)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that "undermine[s] the deposition process" or otherwise "detracts from the just, speedy and inexpensive determination of the interference" contravenes the PTO's administrative objectives (citing 37 C.F.R. § 1.601).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: manufactured evidence prompting extensive investigation, motions to suppress, motions for sanctions, additional conference calls, and rulings that consume APJ time. Such resource expenditures support findings of prejudice to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality debate for false statements to investigators/agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal dispute whether materiality is an essential element for the disciplinary offense of giving false or misleading information to the Office: OED contends materiality is not required because the disciplinary provisions do not reference materiality; respondent argues that materiality is a required element for false-statement offenses, citing cases (e.g., Gaudin, Rigas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: OED's position would permit discipline based on knowingly false statements regardless of whether the falsehood had a material effect on the investigation or outcome; respondent's position requires a showing that the false information was material to the recipient's decision-making or investigation. Model Rules commentary (fraud need not show damage/reliance) is cited by OED as supporting non-materiality in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness to practice includes candor and truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "fitness to practice" has been used in case law to encompass an attorney's disposition to act with integrity, professionalism, and the ability to be candid and truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the Office and adjudicators may interpret statements or prior findings (e.g., adjudicated misrepresentations or an OED letter) as "calling into question" fitness to practice even absent formal charges. Thus, misrepresentations or failures to disclose relevant adverse decisions may be probative of diminished fitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prior adjudications (res judicata / collateral estoppel) in disciplinary inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings by other tribunals (e.g., ITC ID and Federal Circuit affirmance that a practitioner engaged in misrepresentations/inequitable conduct) may be given preclusive effect and can be relied upon in disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order reasoning: the ITC and Federal Circuit determinations regarding misrepresentations to the PTO were not vacated by later settlements or by vacatur of an ALJ recommendation, and doctrines of res judicata/collateral estoppel may bar relitigation of those issues among the parties or those in privity. Such prior findings may support a conclusion that a practitioner's fitness has been called into question.
